newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's labor chieftain seeks post for life.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's labor chieftain seeks post for life.

text.p: Mexico's main labour union met on Monday seeking to muster support for a controversial campaign to make its 96-year-old boss, Fidel Velazquez, leader for the rest of his life.

Velazquez, a quirky ex-milkman who has been a pillar of Mexico's ruling party for the last 50 years, appeared unrivaled in his campaign to lead the 6-million-strong Mexican Workers Confederation (CTM) into the next century.

"More than six million members of the CTM agree on the continuation of F.V. in his post," a banner headline of his newspaper, CTM, said on Monday on the inauguration of the general assembly of Mexico's largest labour confederation.
The vote will be taken next year when Velazquez's eighth consecutive six-year term officially ends.
"He's the only candidate," Javier Pineda, the CTM's secretary of labour told Reuters. "While he is candidate, no one would want to stand against him."

The show of unity behind Don Fidel, as the cigar-chomping leader is known, contrasted with deep fissures in the labour movement as a whole, with many rival unions claiming Velazquez is anti-democratic and a government lackey.
Mexico's wage increases have fallen short of inflation for most of the last 20 years, but Velazquez has mostly avoided strikes, saying labour stability is more beneficial for Mexico.
He is also visibly frail, and it was not clear he would survive a new six-year term as leader that would take him beyond his 100th birthday.
On Monday, Velazquez sat unsmiling as President Ernesto Zedillo praised him at the assembly as "a great Mexican."
He failed to stand up to give the president an embrace at the end of the speech, and was unable to read his own address, asking an assistant to deliver it for him.
However, in his support for Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled Mexico for nearly 68 unbroken years, he was as firm as ever.
During an aside during the assembly, he gloated that the CTM had swung the vote behind its candidate, Alfredo del Mazo, to represent the PRI in the first election for mayor of Mexico City.
He also published a statement to the CTM's rank-and-file setting out in no uncertain terms the way they should vote in the Mexico City and congressional elections on July 6.
"We must make our whole family, our friends and neighbours vote July 6 in favour of the Revolution, in favour of the PRI," the statement, published in full in his newspaper, said.

Whether the CTM manages to force its members to vote for the PRI, as it has done in most elections during the labour group's 61-year history, will be a key test of Velazquez's power in an era of supposedly secret balloting.

There were already indications that his popularity was on the wane. In a defensive editorial, his newspaper noted that the press had orchestrated a "pseudo campaign against our union and our national leader," and it noted that even a government agency had criticised his re-election.
"Six million workers do not accept this attempt to damage his image. Don Fidel is a combatitive and progressive man," the editorial said.
